title: Designing Actionable Alerts
description: Build alerts that fire on user-visible symptoms and route them to the right on-call engineer.

data.text: The on-call rotation is burned out. Alert rules fire dozens of times a day on CPU spikes that nobody can act on, and the team has started ignoring the alert channel. Meanwhile a genuine outage last week was only noticed when a customer tweeted. Redesign the alerting.

Alert on **symptoms, not causes**. Page on error rate and latency budgets that users actually feel; send everything else to a low-urgency channel. Separate alerts into two tiers using **Action Groups** with different notification channels and severities, and use **dynamic thresholds** so a workload with a naturally spiky CPU profile does not page every night.

data.title: Symptom-based alert with an action group (Bicep)
Log-search alert with a latency budget
data.code:
requests
| where timestamp > ago(5m)
| summarize p95 = percentile(duration, 95), total = count() by name
| where total > 20 and p95 > 1500
| project name, p95Ms = p95, total

data.text: CPU at 90% is not a problem; a slow checkout is. Alerts tied to causes produce false positives whenever the workload legitimately gets busy, which trains engineers to ignore the channel — the single most dangerous failure mode in incident response.
